blocks.x: This is an interview with Mr. Charlie Love. We're doing it down on Charter Street with all the doors open in the summertime where it's quite hot. So a lot of street noises on here from the car we hope won't disturb you too much.
Alright Mr. Love can you tell us when you were born and just where? I was born in Blackman, Louisiana on October the 6th, 1885.
What was the first music you remember hearing? Did your father and mother play any instruments?

My father and mother played music together and my sister and my little brother too. He was named Herman Love. Herman Love. Herman, Mary and Nettie. What did your father play? My father played cornet. My mother played the cellar bass. He played what? Cellar bass. Bass? Cellar bass. Cellar bass. Cellar bass. What did they call it? Cellar bass.
Oh the cello you mean? Yeah cellar. The one where you sit down and play? Yeah.

Yeah usually call that cello. Then my father had a band. At that time the fellas used to have meetings. Every time they'd put so much money up until they get enough and they'd buy a set of instruments.
Mm-hm.
He got something to kick out of me. You said you went back to the council and said you got a...

Yeah, I went to the council and he gave me a card, a certificate, you know, a card that they wouldn't hold me up on the border. And he said, now listen, he says, they blowed up the track the other day in Victoria on the way to Monterey and said, you got a chance to go, said they're going to have some soldiers on the train. And I said, we can't guarantee you get there and say, if you want to take a chance, I told him, yeah, I want to take a chance because the band over there, you know, I scared it over there, everybody fighting. So he wrote out the certificate and he told me when I get to Monterey, I had to stop overnight anyhow, to continue to Matamoros the next morning. He said, the hotel right at the station, you go to American Hotel, get your room, he said, six o'clock in the morning when you get on the train going to the border, he said, they'll check your suitcase. They wiped all the marks off, you know, and checked my suitcase. So he said, now when you get to Matamoros, if they ask you why you come from this, tell them you just come from Monterey. And they asked you what you're doing down in Mexico, they're telling you was visiting and playing music at the same time, and you wanted to go home for Christmas. They thought you'd just go home. So they asked me, why you come from Monterey. He told me not to say nothing about Tick, Tamp, they might hold me up, Daniel, for a while.
So I let out for the border.

When I got there, on the Mexico side of the border, they have a Mexican there to search you again. I got there, they searched my baggage and everything. Then they let you go to the middle of the bridge there. They have a United States soldier and a Mexican soldier. You got to take your clothes off. And dress, go in another room and just go all through your clothes, you know. They do that on account of getting dope, you know. They catch people with dope coming from over there. And rip your tire open. And so I passed D9. When I got on the United States side, in Brownsville, Texas, I was satisfied then, you know. All American fellas, but they sure, they had to tell why you was born, how old you was, and who was your mother, your sisters, brothers. And they asked you, do you think you want to go back over there again, you know. I told them, well, I don't live over there. I live in the United States. I'm going home for Christmas. And I said, if I don't find a good job, I may go back over there and work some more. I might, but I said. I made up my mind whether I'm going back or not. I didn't want them to think I was scared, you know. But I was. I was so busy getting home. And you say, well, okay. And I was all right then. I went and got me some cars and rode home, you know, on the border.
You didn't stop in Matamoros to see the sights there?
Matamoros.
Yeah. What happened?
Oh yeah, I stopped when we was going down in there. When we went down there.
Well, if you didn't tell it before, what was Matamoros like? I'd be interested to know.

It's a little, just like the front on Canal Street, you know. Got one big saloon up on the hill. And fellas laying all over the gallery like alligators, you know, loaded. They go over from Brownsville, go over there and drink, you know. And they lay all on the gallery. And when they get tired of drinking, then they come back on Brownsville side and go to sleep. There's no liquor in Brownsville side.
What, did they have any music there?

Oh yeah, all kind of bands. You hear some of the nicest, prettiest music. This little band going around the street playing, they call that Serenable. All kind of pretty. Did you ever hear any mariachis?

Did you ever hear that word? Mariachis, is what they're called? Mariachis. Mariachis. Well, they have stringed instruments mostly, and sometimes a trumpet. They might have a harp, several guitars, different kinds of guitars.
Most of all the little bands I heard that's around the street like that, they use violin, and big guitar, bass violin, and trumpet, sometimes a trombone.
And would they play Mexican music in trombone?

Oh yeah, they're very good musicians. The man that plays pretty music, lovely. I used to like to yell at myself. And many times like that, when I become known over there, and fellas know me, they'd call me to play. Cockless and Murr, any car. Turkey, Turkey Cornet, they'd play a corner with them. And I'd start to play with them and they'd just look at one another. And when I'd get through playing, you know, they'd mark whatever jazz I put in there. Toot-doot-doot-doot, try to get that rhythm, you know.
Did you play the regular Mexican music? Oh yeah.

They're good musicians and they got the music ranged up. Were you ready? Towards last, yeah. Towards last they had got a good job before they blew up that track there. We were going to Mexico City. I had done practiced up with the band. They had a good job there. Twenty dollars a night, all expense paid. Just stay right in the hotel. And tips. Oh, I'd have had some do when I come back there. So the fella had done, made the contract some kind of way. And shortly after that, that's why they blew up the track at Victoria. And then that bust up the trip. And I didn't get a chance to go. That's why I wanted to come home. I just gusted them, you know, that big job there. Twenty dollars a night. No expense. That money's safe. And then tips are so good over there. You make over fifteen or twenty dollars a night tips. That's why I come out of there and come back here. And the time I got back here, Howard Walker come down there with his big old bus. He was getting the band to go to Minnesota. St. Paul, Minnesota. And we picked up some musicians in Jackson, Mississippi. And Memphis. And the entertainer went back to Elligrano for two weeks rehearsing. We rehearsed for two weeks, got the band in shape and left. By the way, St. Louis, we give a dance in Bligh, Arkansas. You know, we'd wake all the way going up. Bligh, Arkansas, and then we went to St. Louis. We'd give a dance in St. Louis. Imperial, Illinois. We'd give a dance there.
Who was in the band then?

Do you remember the name? Howard Walker's band. That fella by the name of Wheaton, Alexander, played alto sack. And they had another young fella. Used to be on the show there. I can't think of his name. Anyway, they had another carnet player. I was playing the second trumpet. This boy had been with Harry Brandt, my old wife, named Charlie, too. Just like me, Charlie Boyer. He was a nice trumpet player. Charlie Boyer. And the trombone player was Ned Mack. And we had Jackson from Mobile, a band-a-play. He was good. Good band-a-play. He was a good band player. And we had Ship on bass. He used to play cornet with Harry a long while ago, right after I had left the band. He played bass. Let me see what drummer we had. Oh yeah, we had this boy familiar, Joe Strutter. He died. He went to Chicago. He didn't come back, the band came back, but he stayed up to his mother who was in Chicago. What did he play?
Drums. He used to play with Lee Collins. Yeah, I remember.

He used to play solo whistle too, you know, play solo whistle, one of them slide and whistles. He was good at that. I'm trying to think of somebody. The fellow was an entertainer, it was with us, was named Rock. They called him Rock.
How do you spell that?
Just like I wrote CK, just like any rock.
Was that like an eight rock?
Yeah, something like that.
Was he a dog? Like an eight rock?
No, he was about my color. He's from Memphis.
They used to call Pigmeat Markham Rock. You know, they used to call him Eight Rock.
Because that was his color.
Did you know that?
This was Brownston fellow, he comes from Memphis.
Did you ever hear Chinese? You know, Abby Foster played slide whistle?

Little Chinese? Yeah, with Celestines Band or anything? I never heard him play the whistle, I heard him play drums. Great cymbal beat, like the beat cymbal and tom-tom. But this boy used to really play that solo. He played a solo just like a man would on a trombone or something.
So what happened with the band? You went on up north with her?

We went on up and after we got up there, we got to St. Paul, Minnesota. We didn't give them no dance there, we went right on in the Chippewa 4. We stopped at the Ottawa Hotel. And the whole time we were there, about two or three days we rehearsed, you know. And the booking agent lived in that town, Mr. Lyons, that's his name, Mr. Lyons. Well, he come down when we got the band all ready, he listened to it. And then we got out on the road then. Steven pointed the highway in, we played all out that way. Waterloo, highway in, turn around and come back. We made some more highway in, then we go over to Milwaukee at the Dell's Ballroom. We played there twice, we played in Wisconsin. And all them little towns, you know, around. And then we come up to have them from Bad Left, the boys had come up to syndicate them, and that boy from Jackson, they wanted to get a smaller band, you know. They were already out on the road and they wanted to get a smaller band and pull out, you know, regular cabaret boys. And I got in on the conversation, it was run, you know. And Lillie Alexander used to play piano with us, you know. What's Alexander? Lillie Milton Alexander. Biscuit's brother, you know that Alexander played the saxophone, he used to play in the band. Adolph, though?
Adolph, yeah, his brother.

Tats. Tats. D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D D Because Joe wanted to stay up that way in Chicago, you see. And they were going to use one corner that the brother was playing in the West Trouble. So they stole the music, that's what gave the whole thing away. Harry had about $25 to $30 worth of new music. Which belonged to him personally. And when we went to bed in a little town, up around the highway there somewhere, the boys went to bed and stole the music. So we went to the lines, you see. We had a big job to play in, what's the capital of Wisconsin? Madison. Yeah, we had to play in Madison on a big job. Had to sign a contract, made a contract and everything. So these boys stole the music that night. When we went over there to play this big job with the big band, they wasn't going no further with Harry and they ain't going to take that job, you see. Well, we had to come back. And me and Harry, they had to come back and get shipped. Three of us would have to come back to the other guy. They didn't want Harry, they didn't want me, and they didn't want Ship. They didn't want to use no bass. So I told him, I said, don't you fool with them fellas.
I said, I'm kind of on that sand to keep that now. I said, the best thing you can do.

I said, that's a nice fella. You know, I worked with Harry for years. I said, and Ellick was kind of scared. He said, well, before you get mad and I'm way up here, don't bring me home. I said, I'm the one that look out for you. Your daddy told me to look out for you. I said, you're not going with them fellas. And he fooled on. He said, well, you think I ought to tell Harry? I said, that's the thing you should do. Tell him. Tell him what them fellas is fixing to do. And I said, he said, well, I took $35 from him. They give me, give me mean wheat. They're going to take Harris. And I said, well, I took $35 from him. They give me dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear know what it's all about you know. Take his saxophone player. Yeah he's gonna take his player. And he told me that you know I said well you go tell Harry this is what them boys gonna do. I said that's a nice fella. I said you might want to play with him again you know. And I said you going back to New Orleans. I said he's gonna take us back to New Orleans just like he come down there and got us. I said that's a gentleman. So Alexander told him you know and then I come up with him. I told Harry I said yeah you got a syndicate on there. You better look out for yourself you know. And Mr. Lyons he went back home to Chippewa Falls you know and he come pick the band up the next day. Harry said Mr. Lyons. He said I owe you about $15. I said there's your $15. I said now you owe for the gas this week. He said I'd like a settlement. Mr. Lyons said why you want a settlement? He said well that's the way I run business. I don't get my business right. I done paid my debt now I want you to pay me for the gas. Got the money for the gas and everything you know. So we so busy getting away from that town the highway we loaded up you know. And this Sunday kid done quit riding with us. He's riding Mr. Lyons in his car you know. Great big car. Harry said uh-huh I see what they're doing. So we lit out you know. So Harry said where's the music at? He said look here. I said we got to stop and get our music. That's it. I got too much music in there to lose. So Harry said I'm going to stop in this next town and get that music. So we when we got to that next town there was a sheriff there waiting for us. Waitin' for me, Harry, and the ship. And Wheat and Alexander. He was waitin' for us you know. He said of course I ain't got no charge against you. I can't arrest you boys but them fellas say y'all took their music you know. Y'all got the music. I said yeah then. I took it as my own property. They said they stole it from me and hid it on the mattress. He said I got the music back. He said well I'd like for y'all to drive to the curb Dan. He said you're not rustic or nothin' you can go on and eat some buckets or whatever you know. I told them fellas get Juddy right behind y'all they oughta be here in about a half an hour. So we waited man. Then the big thing come on and went over to the city hall. And Harry told the chief police you know all about it say. Well the fellas syndicated on me. He said we had a contract in Madison to play. He said but now I don't want none of it say. I've been a musician all my life. He said love yeah he's been with me. And Chip took love to play when love didn't play cornet the more I used ship on the bass. He said this fella young. I raised him in Alexander my saxophone player said they had him too. And he even bribed them. Give them $35. Told them if they didn't like the job they could come back on the cushions. He said now I don't want none of it and I'm gonna bring these boys back where I got them from. And Rock wanted to speak that Hebrew from Memphis. He said well Harry I don't want to go back down there no more. I'm stay back up north. You know I ain't going down there no more. Harry said I ain't got nothing to do with you at all. He said I'll come and got you in Memphis and I'll bring you back home if you want to go home. So if you want to stay up there with them you can go head on and stay but Alexander is going home with love. And Wheat I'll take care of him. Wheat cause I raised this boy. And he said shit don't want nothing to do with it. And he said I'm through. Harry said I can see you in the jail doors yearning for me. I'll quit. He said because I never been arrested in my life. Never been in no trouble. Never give nobody no trouble. And so the sheriff spoke you know. They said well I'll tell you what you do. Why don't you boys just go and finish that engagement and then quit after that and go home. dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Oh yeah, I heard about him.
You were telling about Brunk up in Alexandria. How did he play then?

He played all right but just that old way like we used to play around there years ago, you know like Buddy Bowling and that's during Buddy Pete's time you see. He was a very nice little trumpet player, played by air though he never did read nothing about it. Buddy Petite. Yeah.
Do you think that Brunk imitated Buddy Petite?

No he didn't imitate, he was a better cornet player in Buddy Petite I think. Brunk was a better cornet player than Buddy Petite. He knew a little something about music you see. Uh huh. And Buddy didn't know nothing about music. That made Brunk the best. Did you ever play in the same band with Bunk any place? Oh yeah I played around there with him on jobs, you know, a little gig job some time. I played with him in Alexandria. And got a job for him, got a job for him and Clarence William and Paul, a fellow with rope keeping up and you can't come in. Paul Weyer. He's from Pensacola, Florida. That's Paul. That guy was a crack shot on the violin.
The violin? Wasn't he with Handy once too?
Oh yeah he played with Handy and his brother was a violin player too. He was good but he was a big gambler.
How do you spell his name? Paul? Do you remember Paul's last name? Paul. Wasn't it?
I got some sheet music, I got all that sheet music.
Yeah it seems to me there was a clarinet player that was related to him or something. I got some sheet music. Yeah well we'll look at it. He had a band in Pensacola.

Yeah. Him and his brother, they had a band there. Well I guess all them fellas played together. He was a good violin player. He used to come around where our band was, you know, we had a little joint where we used to sit around there until it was time to go to work. We was working over the bar there. And he'd come in, you know, and we heard he was violin playing the news, gambling all the time, you know, and said, say, Pensacola, do you mind playing a little violin for us? He said, yeah I'd play for you but I ain't got no violin. He said, I'll get you one. He said, sure I'll play. So they gave him the violin, you know, they thought they was going to have some fun. And we asked them to play. He said, what you want me to play for you? He said, can you play like Calvary? He went right on into it. Played the whole thing better than we could, by itself. I said, well, I'm in class. He said, uh-huh, you see that, eh? Then they asked him for several other pieces to play there. Raymond, he played Raymond. I said, that guy's a violin player. So we tried to get him to work over the bar while we was working, you know. He said, uh, Pensacola, you want to work? He said, no, man, I don't want to work. He said, I can take these and make all the money I want to put out a bag dice, you know. He was full of tricks. He was a pool shark, you know. Yeah. So they had a pool table in there while we was at, you know, in that place, you know. He got to talking with the fellas and he stole the chalk, stole the tall ball. His fellas wanted to play and couldn't find the tall ball, you know. The fellas would go to the kids and say, look in that fellas' pocket right there. They went over there and looked and the fellas had the tall ball there, you know. And they all got scared of him and they were so full of tricks, you know. They make it disappear, throw it out on the table, you know.
What kind of ball was that?
A pool ball. Pool table. Oh, I see.
Oh, did you ever run into Jolly Row Martin, the Wyandand boy?

Jolly Row Martin, I know him well. I used to play with him too. Where? He was from Monroe, Monroe, Louisiana. He was around Shreeport. When we had the band there, he used to come around and sit around, you know, and play something. He'd be working on a job like that. He'd tell the fellas, get up, let me play something. He'd get up and he'd play something, you know. That's the way the musicians were.
Did he play pool a lot in those days, do you remember? Huh? Did Jolly Row play pool much in those days too? Pool?

Yeah. Yeah. He used to play pool, around Shreeport. And Pensacola kid would come into town like Alexander, you see, and he'd find out who's the best pool player in town and he'd lay around for a big game, you see. And when he'd get that big game, he'd fixin' to leave there then, you know, about $150 or two, $300. He's going to win that. He'd make the ball any way he want, any time, steal it, anything. And so when he left Alexander, he disappeared and we went to Chicago. We found him there running a pool hall for a fellow.
He was in Chicago.

But that guy is a really violent player. And that tune come out, you know, about keep a knockin' and you can't come in, you know. I heard that thing before, you know. I heard it and I said, I know that piece. I've heard that somewhere. And I met him, you know. He told me that was by him. He made that piece. I didn't believe it. But I found out later that it was a hit to him. There ain't nothin' to it, but it was a hit. Everybody liked it.
Do you know any of the words to it?
No, I didn't know anymore. Keep knockin' and you can't come in. It's a kind of a spoody song, you know.
And they called, that was Paul Weyer, the violin player. Paul Weyer. They called him Pensacola Kid.
Pensacola Kid. Did he play piano?
I thought Pensacola Kid was a pianist. No, he was a violin.

Never did play piano. He was a cat with a violin. I don't know, he might have could play piano, but I never did know him as a piano player. Well, Finney's telling him, I got this boy a job, Pensacola Kid, Clarence William, and Bunk Johnson. And Baby Lovett was playing with us. We let him have Baby and we took another drummer. Took little Jack Hine, that was Baby's friend. So they all went down and worked at this house together. They had a nice band. We could be on playing, you know, at night. Where were they playing?
What was the place? Huh? What was the place called where they worked? You know one name. Or house, wasn't it?
The house, yeah. Dance hall house. The dance hall with the girls too, huh? Yeah, with the girls.
Regular school. Eighteen girls and, uh.
Excuse me. Sure. Suppose I put the... Well, let's see, you were talking about that job there at Bunk and All Play.

Uh, Bunk and they were playing in a place, what town was that I got lost? Yeah, it was the only town across the Bayer. Why'd they call it that? Across the Bayer or something? It was across. Bayer Rapide. Right across on the other side.
Uh huh. Like a little island over there. Uh huh. Nothing but fast. Help people. I got the picture. Of it now. And that's where Bunk, Dineswil, Paul Wilde, David Luggan.
That's where they was, that's where they was working at.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. You see, the man just left. They got scared. Yeah. They got on the train. David Lovett was going to leave there too, but Dr. Brown knew them very well, you know, and went and got him. They got his ticket and everything. That was waiting down and said, you can't run off from home like that. You're going to stay home. What was David Lovett from? Bunk left from around Alexander then. He must have come back here. And shortly after that, he went to Houston. Oh Lord. Shortly after that, he went to Houston. I saw him. Uh-uh.
You got something locked.

Yeah, I'll get him locked after a while. Where were we then? Bunk left Alexander. He must have come back here, and then he went to Houston. I never heard of him anymore then until I saw him back there in Northern Michigan.
Remember about what year that was when Bunk was up there?
Around, around Alexander? Mm-hmm. 1908.
Mm-hmm. Way back. Did you ever get into New Orleans in those days, even for a day or two or a night to hear a little bit of music down here or anything at all?
I had to just had to put on pants.
Mm-hmm.
Just a little bit of . Boy, I used to live here, you know.
Well, you live down here too?

My cousin stayed there, Miss Bank. She's in G bamboo now. Mm-hmm. live right down on that canal there. What year was that you first started coming to town? That was way back. Maybe my wife might tell you the exact year, because she was born in Napoleonville, but she was raised up around there as a baby.
Anyway, you were just a little boy then.

When I got to be a young man, when the music business failed on me, you know, there wasn't much to do, I come down here to learn more music and work on the first building to put that media down. Over here in Algeria. Yeah, I asked a man for a job and he laughed at me. He said, we hired men over here, we ain't hired no babies. And I just hang around there, you know, every day, and I heard him whispering, you know, say, I'll be that boy that do want to work, you know. Do it up a little bit. He said, that's all right. He said, I believe I'm going to give you a job. Can you roll one of them wheel barrels like you see them fellas doing there? I said, sure, I can do that. I can do anything. He said, well, get your wheel barrel. And I got a wheel barrel that was mixed in concrete up on a, on a mat then. And that's the way they used to mix that stuff, you know. It took a great big fella man with muscles, you know, to turn that stuff over, you know. Well, I couldn't do no mixing but I could roll it after they mixed it up. Man, I was getting all fine at that time. At that time they was paying $2.82 a day from 6 in the morning until 4 in the evening. I used to get my lunch, my cousin would fix my lunch, and I'd go out there and make a day just like the rest of them fellas. So they'd come in. You know fellas play on all jobs, they'd come in to get the kicks out of me, you know. Every time they'd go to mix up a batch of that concrete, I had a way of, I know I was too light, I'd just go sit down and look at them and mix it. When they get through them I'd get my wheel barrel, fall in line and start to, oh, and them fellas used to kid, you know, say, say, boy, you can't sit down on this job. I said, boy, man, see you do that man, see you ain't got no job, you're fired, see you have to get your shovels, help them mix this stuff up, you don't want to get a kick, you know. I'd grab a shovel well in the wake, you know, rolling up on there and couldn't turn it over enough, kick up on the side. So I said, man, you don't mix it that way, you got to have muscle like that and turn it over. And the boss man, I looked around and seen him laughing, you know, he just said, he's killing himself laughing, he turned his back and said, say, fella, come here. I went over there, he said, them fellas try to kid me, he said, they're kidding me, he said, you can't mix that stuff, we got special women to do that, them big fellas there, say, go sit down until they get through. I went and sat down, I was over waking myself, you know, trying to mix that concrete. Say I was wondering, when was the first time you ever?
I was wondering, yeah then.

Well at that time, Peter Buchhosh was playing guitar with Charlie DeVoges. He was a professor like mine. That's all down there on that canal down there. I was living there, right by the graveyard, I was living there with my cousin, little bit of fella, you know, call myself and they can plant him on there.
Is that the Whitney Avenue canal or Whitney Avenue, that canal you're talking about or what avenue?

Yeah. That's on New Nez, on New Nez Street. Oh yeah. That's big canal there. And a graveyard right by the, I lived in that last house, right by the graveyard. I used to go in the early that night, I was scared, you know. Scared of ghosts. I was a little boy, I remember that this as well, and I got sick. And they sent me, my cousin sent me back to Plackham, to my mother, you see. I got around there and got me up a nut, little man, started playing around there. And I learned a boy how to play, they called him Sidney Williams. He made a nice trumpet player, but he's dead now.
When was the first time you ever heard Louis Armstrong and Kid René in those songs?

When I was a little boy. He'd come to Plackham, Rennie and Black Benny and all them, you know the drummer that's called Brass Band. Had some little girls in the band. They had a big brass band, you know. Something on the other, John Caggill's band. But they had more in that band. They had little peck horns, you know, and tenors, upright tenors. Made like a baritone. They had baritone and a little bit of old cornets, looked like a funner, you know. Louis was the leader of that band. They come to Plackham and I went up there and got with them and played and wanted to come to New Orleans with that band. You know, I thought that was a fine band at that time. Papa said, boys, you crazy? You want to go to jail? I said, them bad boys, they in the house there. See, you ain't got a bitter sense of that.
What age were you? I don't know.
I was about around ten years old. I believe.
